q: Which agency issues Nevada real estate licenses and investigates complaints?
wrong: A trade association can't issue licenses.
The Attorney General doesn't run licensing.
why: NRED licenses real estate professionals and investigates violations.

q: The Nevada Real Estate Division is part of which state department?
why: NRED is a division of the Department of Business and Industry.

q: Members of the Nevada Real Estate Commission are appointed by:
wrong: The Legislature passes laws but doesn't appoint Commissioners.
why: The Governor appoints the Commission.

q: Which is a main role of the Real Estate Commission?
options: Adopting regulations and deciding disciplinary cases
wrong: No government body sets commission rates; they're negotiable.
why: The Commission makes rules and hears discipline cases.

q: The official who heads the Real Estate Division is the:
wrong: The Commission is separate from the Division's leadership.
The AG is the state's lawyer.
The Ombudsman serves common-interest community owners.
why: The Administrator runs the Division's operations.

q: What is NAC 645?
options: Regulations adopted under Nevada's real estate license law
wrong: Codes of ethics are association rules.
why: NAC 645 contains the regulations; NRS 645 is the statute.
hook: NRS is the law. NAC fills in the details.

q: The Nevada Real Estate Commission sets the commission rates licensees must charge.
wrong: Commissions are negotiable between brokers and clients.
why: False.

q: The Real Estate Division can investigate a licensee after receiving a complaint.
wrong: Investigating complaints is a core Division function.
why: True.

q: A Division investigator asks a broker to produce trust account records. The broker should:
options: Ask the client's permission before responding
wrong: Brokers must make records available to the Division.
Destroying records is a serious violation.
Client permission isn't required for a lawful Division request.
why: Nevada law lets the Division inspect and audit broker records.

q: How many members serve on the Nevada Real Estate Commission?
wrong: [verify] The Commission is generally described as having five members.
why: The Commission is commonly described as five members appointed by the Governor. [verify on NRED before relying on this]

q: You're unsure whether a marketing idea complies with Nevada rules. What should the agent do?
options: Check NRS and NAC 645 and ask your broker before using it
Do it and wait to see if anyone complains
Rely on what another state allows
wrong: Waiting for a complaint invites discipline.
why: Nevada's statutes, regulations, and your broker are the right sources.
hook: When in doubt, ask your broker.

q: Which of these does the Real Estate Division handle?
options: Issuing licenses and approving real estate education
wrong: Tax rates are set by government bodies, not NRED.
why: NRED licenses professionals and oversees real estate education.

q: Violating a regulation in NAC 645 can lead to discipline just like violating the statute.
wrong: Regulations have the force of law for licensees.
why: True.
hook: NRS is the law. NAC fills in the details.

q: Common-interest community matters, like HOA manager regulation, fall under a separate body within the Division called the:
options: Commission for Common-Interest Communities and Condominium Hotels
wrong: The Real Estate Commission oversees real estate licensees.
why: Nevada has a separate commission for CIC and condo hotel matters.

q: The Real Estate Commission may fine a licensee up to how much per violation?
why: Nevada allows administrative fines of up to $10,000 for each violation.

q: Which is NOT a discipline the Commission can impose?
why: The Commission imposes administrative discipline. Criminal penalties come from courts.

q: A licensee disagrees with the Commission's final disciplinary order. The licensee may:
options: Petition a district court for judicial review
Ask the MLS to overturn it
Appeal to the local REALTOR® association
wrong: The MLS has no authority over discipline.
Ignoring an order brings more penalties.
why: Final agency decisions can be reviewed by a district court.
hook: Disagree? Go to court, not the MLS.

q: Put the typical disciplinary steps in order.
options: A complaint is filed with the Division
The case is heard by the Commission
why: Complaint, investigation, hearing, then decision.

q: A licensee is found to have committed three separate violations. The maximum total fine could be:
wrong: Exceeds three times the per-violation cap.
why: At up to $10,000 per violation, three violations could total $30,000.

q: A licensee accused of a violation has a chance to respond before the Commission decides.
wrong: Due process includes notice and an opportunity to be heard.
why: True.

q: A broker can be disciplined for failing to supervise a salesperson who broke the law.
wrong: Failure to supervise is itself a violation.
why: True.
hook: The broker answers for the team.

q: You receive notice from the Division that a client filed a complaint against you. What should the agent do?
options: Tell your broker, gather your records, respond honestly and on time, and consider legal advice
Ignore it, since the client is wrong
Call the client and pressure them to withdraw it
Change your records to look better
wrong: Ignoring a Division notice can bring additional discipline.
why: Respond promptly and honestly with your broker's involvement.

q: Who may file a complaint against a Nevada licensee with the Division?
options: Only a client who paid a commission
wrong: Customers and others can complain too.
why: Anyone can bring a complaint to the Division.

q: A licensee is disciplined by the Commission for misrepresentation. The harmed buyer:
options: May still sue the licensee in civil court for damages
Is automatically paid by the Commission
wrong: The Commission doesn't pay damages; the Recovery Fund has its own process.
Discipline doesn't bar a civil suit.
why: Discipline and civil liability are separate.

q: Revocation of a license means:
options: The licensee pays a small fine
The license is paused for 30 days
The licensee must take one class
why: Revocation cancels the license; suspension temporarily stops it.

q: A person without a license who performs licensed real estate activity can face penalties under Nevada law.
wrong: Unlicensed activity is unlawful and can carry penalties.
why: True.
hook: For others, for pay? Get licensed.

q: A formal written statement of disapproval issued as discipline is a:
wrong: A Recovery Fund claim compensates victims.
A cease and desist orders someone to stop activity.
why: A reprimand is a formal censure.

q: The Commission fines a licensee the maximum for each of two violations. What is the total fine?
formula: Total = number of violations × maximum fine per violation
why: Two violations at $10,000 each is $20,000.

q: The Real Estate Education, Research and Recovery Fund mainly pays:
options: People who won uncollectible judgments against licensees for fraud, misrepresentation or deceit
wrong: The Fund doesn't pay lost commissions.
why: The Fund compensates victims of licensee fraud who can't collect their judgment.
hook: Win in court first, then apply to the Fund.

q: Before applying to the Recovery Fund, a harmed person generally must:
options: Obtain a court judgment against the licensee
Wait for the licensee to retire
wrong: The MLS isn't part of the process.
why: A judgment based on fraud, misrepresentation or deceit is the starting point.

q: The commonly cited maximum the Recovery Fund pays for any one judgment is:
wrong: That's the fine cap, not the Fund limit.
That's the commonly cited per-licensee total.
why: The Fund is commonly described as paying up to $25,000 per judgment. [verify current limit on NRED]

q: The commonly cited maximum the Recovery Fund pays on claims involving a single licensee is:
why: Claims involving one licensee are commonly capped at $100,000 total. [verify current limit on NRED]

q: When the Recovery Fund pays a claim based on a licensee's conduct, the licensee's license:
options: Is suspended until the licensee repays the Fund with interest
wrong: There are consequences for the licensee.
why: The licensee must repay the Fund, with interest, before practicing again.
hook: The Fund pays; the licensee pays it back.

q: As its name says, the Fund also supports real estate education and research.
wrong: The Fund serves education, research, and recovery.
why: True.

q: The Recovery Fund pays any claim against a licensee, including simple disagreements over commission.
wrong: The Fund covers judgments based on fraud, misrepresentation or deceit in a transaction, not ordinary business disputes.
why: False.

q: A buyer holds an uncollectible $40,000 fraud judgment against a licensee. Using the commonly cited $25,000 per-judgment limit, what is the most the Fund would pay?
formula: Payout = the lesser of the unpaid actual damages or the per-judgment limit
steps: The Fund pays the lower amount: $25,000.
why: The Fund pays up to its limit, not the full judgment. [verify current limit]

q: A past client was defrauded by another licensee and asks whether the Recovery Fund can help. What should the agent do?
options: Explain the Fund exists, that a court judgment is generally required first, and suggest they speak with an attorney and contact the Division
Promise the Fund will pay in full
Say the Fund only helps licensees
File a claim for them without their involvement
wrong: Payouts are capped and require a process.
You can't file legal claims on their behalf.
why: Point them to the process and the right professionals.
hook: Win in court first, then apply to the Fund.

q: Five victims each hold $25,000 fraud judgments against the same licensee. Using the commonly cited limits, the total the Fund would pay for all of them is at most:
wrong: The per-licensee cap limits the total.
why: Total payments for one licensee are capped at the aggregate limit, commonly $100,000. [verify]

q: A licensee whose conduct caused a Fund payment must repay the amount plus interest to have the license reinstated.
why: True.
hook: The Fund pays; the licensee pays it back.

q: How is the Recovery Fund mainly financed?
wrong: Buyers don't fund it at closing.
why: Licensees pay into the Fund through licensing fees.

q: Recovery Fund payments are generally based on:
options: The claimant's unpaid actual damages, up to the limits
why: The Fund pays unpaid actual damages within the limits.

q: The Recovery Fund exists to protect the public.
wrong: It compensates consumers harmed by licensee fraud.
why: True.

q: Which activity requires a Nevada real estate license?
options: Negotiating the sale of a neighbor's home for a fee
wrong: Owners may sell their own property.
Buying for yourself doesn't require a license.
Owners renting their own property don't need one.
why: Acting for others for compensation requires a license.
hook: For others, for pay? Get licensed.

q: An unlicensed person who helped arrange a sale sues for a commission. In Nevada, generally:
options: They can't recover a commission because they weren't licensed
They can recover if the seller agreed in writing
They can recover if the sale closed
wrong: A written agreement doesn't cure the lack of a license.
why: Only licensees can sue to collect compensation for licensed activity.
hook: No license, no lawsuit for pay.

q: A licensee pays a friend $500 for finding a buyer the friend negotiated with. The friend isn't licensed. This is:
options: A violation for paying an unlicensed person for licensed activity
Allowed if disclosed to the seller
wrong: Paying for negotiating is paying for licensed activity.
why: Licensees may not pay unlicensed people for licensed work.
hook: Never pay the unlicensed for licensed work.

q: Which person generally doesn't need a real estate license to sell property in that role?
options: An executor selling under court authority
A friend selling for a fee
An unlicensed assistant negotiating for an agent
A relative listing homes for neighbors
wrong: Selling for others for a fee requires a license.
Assistants can't negotiate without a license.
Listing for others requires a license.
why: Court-appointed fiduciaries acting in that role are generally exempt. [verify exemption list]
hook: Your own property, or by court order.

q: An owner can sell their own Nevada home without a real estate license.
wrong: Owners dealing with their own property are exempt.
why: True.
hook: Your own property, no license needed.

q: Merely offering to list or sell property for others for compensation can count as licensed activity.
wrong: Offering or attempting is included in licensed activity.
why: True.

q: Your unlicensed assistant offers to show a home and discuss price while you're busy. What should the agent do?
options: Say no; showing with price discussion and negotiation is licensed activity
Allow it if the buyer agrees
Let them show it but not take questions
wrong: Unlicensed activity isn't allowed even once.
Showing and engaging buyers about the property is licensed work.
why: Unlicensed staff can't perform licensed activities.

q: Someone who leases apartments for several owners for a fee in Nevada must generally have:
options: A real estate license, and a property management permit for property management
wrong: Leasing for others for pay is licensed activity.
why: Leasing for others requires a license, and property management requires a permit.

q: A broker licensed only in California wants to list a Las Vegas home. Generally they must:
options: Work with a Nevada-licensed broker as Nevada law allows, or get a Nevada license
List it freely because licenses are national
Use a California listing agreement only
wrong: Licenses are issued by each state.
The location of the property controls.
why: Real estate activity in Nevada requires Nevada licensure or a cooperative arrangement allowed by Nevada law.

q: A real estate license from another state automatically lets you practice in Nevada.
why: False.

q: The Division learns someone is advertising homes for sale for others without a license. The Division can:
options: Take action, including ordering the person to stop and seeking penalties
Do nothing because the person isn't licensed
Refer it only to the MLS
wrong: Unlicensed activity is within the Division's enforcement.
The MLS has no enforcement role.
why: The Division can act against unlicensed activity. [verify specific remedies]
hook: For others, for pay? Get licensed.

q: Helping someone else buy a home for a fee requires:
options: Nothing, if the buyer is a friend
why: Representing buyers for compensation is licensed activity.
hook: For others, for pay? Get licensed.

q: A licensee may pay a referral fee to an unlicensed person for referring a client.
wrong: Nevada prohibits paying unlicensed persons compensation for licensed activity. [verify specific referral rules]
why: False.
hook: Never pay the unlicensed for licensed work.

q: A friend who isn't licensed says, "Send me a cut if my coworker buys through you." What should the agent do?
options: Decline to pay, and explain that Nevada law doesn't allow paying unlicensed people for real estate work
Agree and run it through the title company
wrong: Routing it differently doesn't change what it is.
why: Paying unlicensed persons for real estate work can bring discipline.
hook: Never pay the unlicensed for licensed work.

q: A Nevada salesperson may perform real estate activities only:
options: While associated with and supervised by a licensed broker
wrong: A business license doesn't replace broker supervision.
There's no five-year rule for this.
why: Salespeople must work under a broker.

q: A person who meets broker qualifications but works under another broker holds a:
wrong: A salesperson hasn't met broker qualifications.
A permit isn't a license class.
A permit isn't a license class.
why: Broker-salespersons have broker qualifications but work under a broker.

q: A Nevada licensee who wants to engage in property management must have:
wrong: Nevada requires a permit for property management.
why: Property management in Nevada requires a permit.

q: A licensee who helps clients buy and sell businesses needs a:
wrong: Business brokerage in Nevada uses a business broker permit.
why: Business brokerage requires a permit in Nevada.
hook: Selling businesses? Get the business broker permit.

q: A broker can operate their own brokerage and supervise other licensees.
wrong: That's what a broker license allows.
why: True.

q: A salesperson may open an office in their own name and hire other salespeople.
wrong: Only brokers can operate brokerages and supervise licensees.
why: False.

q: A property management permit is best described as:
options: An addition to a real estate license that allows property management
A separate license that doesn't require a real estate license
A permit only for HOA managers
wrong: The permit builds on a real estate license.
HOA managers have a separate certification.
why: The permit is held in addition to a license.
hook: Permit on top of a license.

q: A buyer client asks you to manage their new rental after closing. You hold only a salesperson license. What should the agent do?
options: Explain you need a property management permit, and refer them to a permitted manager or get the permit through your broker first
Manage it but don't charge a fee
wrong: Managing without the permit is a violation.
Unpaid informal management can still cause problems; the permit rule applies to property management activity.
Your spouse would need proper licensing too.
why: Property management needs the permit.

q: Who supervises a broker-salesperson?
wrong: The Commission regulates; it doesn't supervise daily work.
why: Broker-salespersons are supervised by their broker.

q: Managing a homeowners association in Nevada is regulated separately from residential property management.
wrong: HOA community managers have their own certification under a separate chapter.
why: True. Community association managers are certified separately. [verify]

q: Which list contains Nevada real estate license types?
wrong: REALTOR® is a trademark, not a license.
why: Nevada licenses salespersons, broker-salespersons, and brokers.

q: A new licensee wants to call themselves a REALTOR® on their business cards. They must:
options: Be a member of the National Association of REALTORS® through a local association
wrong: The term isn't tied to license class.
The Division doesn't grant the trademark.
why: REALTOR® is a membership trademark, not a license type.
hook: Licensed by the state; REALTOR® by membership.

q: A broker-salesperson may run an independent brokerage while associated with another broker.
wrong: A broker-salesperson works under their associated broker, not independently.
why: False.

q: To get a property management permit, a licensee generally must:
options: Complete required property management education and apply to the Division
Just pay a fee to the county
wrong: The Division issues the permit after education requirements.
why: Permits require specific education and an application. [verify hours]

q: Pre-licensing education for a Nevada salesperson must be completed:
options: At a school or provider approved by the Real Estate Division
On the job with a broker
wrong: On-the-job training doesn't replace required courses.
why: Only NRED-approved education counts.
hook: Approved school, or it doesn't count.

q: Put the usual steps to a Nevada salesperson license in order.
options: Register with NRED and pass the Pearson VUE exam
Get fingerprinted for the background check
Submit the license application with a sponsoring broker
why: Education, exam, fingerprints, then application. Check current Division rules for timing.

q: Why does Nevada require fingerprints from license applicants?
why: Fingerprints support a background check.

q: An applicant has a past conviction. On the license application, they should:
options: Disclose it as required and provide requested documents
Leave it off and hope it isn't found
Disclose it only if asked in an interview
Wait until after licensing to mention it
wrong: Hiding it can lead to denial for dishonesty.
Late disclosure can lead to discipline.
why: Honest disclosure lets the Division evaluate it; concealment is a separate problem.
hook: Disclose it before they find it.

q: To qualify for a salesperson license, the applicant must pass:
options: Both the National and Nevada State portions of the exam
No exam if they finish the course
wrong: The State portion is required too.
The National portion is required too.
why: Both portions must be passed.

q: A study app like YPFG Academy counts toward Nevada's required pre-licensing education hours.
wrong: Only NRED-approved courses count toward the required hours.
why: False. That's why the app shows its disclaimer.
hook: Approved school, or it doesn't count.

q: Passing exam results stay valid for a limited time, so applicants should apply promptly.
wrong: Exam results expire if you don't apply in time. [verify period]
why: True. See the Roadmap for the current period.

q: Under the current process, before scheduling the Pearson VUE exam a Nevada candidate must:
options: Register and pay through the NRED website
Get a broker to schedule it
why: Since July 29, 2025, candidates register and pay through NRED before scheduling. [verify]

q: A licensing candidate asks when to get fingerprinted. What's the best general advice?
options: Check NRED's current requirements; fingerprints expire, so time them close to submitting the application
Do it on day one of school
Do it after the license is issued
wrong: Early prints may expire before you apply.
They're needed to issue the license.
why: Fingerprint results expire, so timing matters. See your Roadmap.
hook: Time your prints to your application.

q: To receive an active salesperson license, the applicant must:
options: Be associated with a sponsoring broker
why: Active salesperson licenses require broker association.

q: Nevada applicants must meet a minimum age requirement to be licensed.
wrong: There's a minimum age. See the Roadmap for the figure to verify.
why: True.

q: The Division discovers an applicant made a false statement on their application. Likely result:
options: Denial of the license, or later discipline if already issued
why: Honesty is a licensing requirement.
hook: Disclose it before they find it.

citation: Pearson VUE Nevada Candidate Handbook [verify citation]
q: Who administers the Nevada real estate license exam?
options: Pearson VUE, under contract with the state
wrong: Schools teach; they don't give the state exam.
why: Pearson VUE delivers the Nevada exam.

q: An applicant can receive a Nevada salesperson license before passing the exam if their broker vouches for them.
wrong: Passing the exam is required before licensure.
why: False.

q: A salesperson whose license is inactive may:
options: Not perform real estate activities for others
Show homes if a broker is present
wrong: Licensed activity is still licensed activity.
why: Inactive licenses don't permit practice.

q: A salesperson leaves their brokerage. Until they associate with a new broker through the Division, they:
options: Can keep working their current deals alone
Can work as an unlicensed assistant to negotiate
wrong: Working without a broker isn't allowed.
why: A salesperson must be associated with a broker to practice.

q: After the first renewal, Nevada licensees commonly need how many hours of continuing education per two-year renewal?
why: Most sources cite 36 hours per two-year cycle, with required topics. [verify on NRED]

q: New Nevada salespersons must complete post-licensing education:
options: During their first year of licensure
why: Post-licensing happens in the first year. [verify hours]
hook: First year: post-licensing. Every cycle: CE.

q: Nevada CE includes required topics such as:
wrong: Marketing alone doesn't meet the required topics.
why: Required CE categories cover core legal and ethical topics. [verify current categories]

q: A licensee who hasn't completed required CE can't renew an active license.
wrong: CE is a renewal requirement for active status.
why: True.

q: Post-licensing courses can also be counted as continuing education.
wrong: Sources indicate post-licensing courses aren't accepted as CE. [verify]
why: False.

q: Your license renewal date passed while you were finishing CE. What should the agent do?
options: Stop practicing until the license is properly renewed or reinstated, and follow the Division's late-renewal process
Have your broker sign for you
wrong: Practicing on an expired license is unlicensed activity.
Using someone else's license is a serious violation.
why: An expired license can't be used. Follow the Division's process.

q: To reactivate an inactive license, a licensee generally must:
options: Meet CE requirements and associate with a broker through the Division
Get a new Social Security number
wrong: Reactivation requires more than a payment.
Pre-licensing usually isn't repeated for reactivation.
why: Reactivation requires current education and broker association. [verify details]
hook: Catch up on CE, find a broker.

q: After the initial license period, Nevada licenses generally renew:
why: Nevada uses a two-year renewal cycle after the initial period. [verify]

q: Changing brokerages requires a change of association processed through the Division.
wrong: The Division must process the new association.
why: True.

q: When a salesperson changes brokerages, their pending listings generally:
why: Brokerage agreements belong to the broker.

q: Nevada CE rules may require some hours to be completed through live instruction.
wrong: Sources describe a live-instruction requirement for part of CE. [verify]
why: True. [verify current rule]

q: If a licensee's contact information or business address changes, they should:
wrong: The Division must also have current information.
why: Licensees keep their Division records current. [verify deadline]
